The Commons Fridge2026MA final project

Make shared care easier to negotiate.

Five habit interviews redirected a full-inventory concept toward lighter shared coordination: see the item, understand ownership, then decide what can be done.

Problem
In a shared flat, the trouble with one fridge is not only forgotten food: people hesitate to remind each other, the same person ends up tidying, and nobody is sure whose things can be touched.
Key decisions
I dropped the full-inventory idea and designed for four moments only: putting something in, checking and handling, before shopping, and finding something. Where an item is, whose it is and what others may do are three separate things; an unclaimed item stays “not sure whose”.
Outcome
A working bilingual prototype, and NFC entry points on the fridge door.
Context
University of Southampton · MA final project
My role
Research, system design, interactions, prototype & product decisions
Period
2026
Delivery
Physical touchpoints, bilingual prototype, demonstration; v2.0 multi-tenant build, trialled in a five-person shared flat

01 · Research

The friction is social as well as practical.

I conducted five interviews about existing shared-fridge habits. The problems went beyond forgotten items: hesitation about reminding someone, recurring care work falling to one person, and repeated conflict around unclear boundaries.

U02 worried that a group message could sound like a complaint; U01 carried the work of checking and organising; U05 described how boundaries and capacity pressure affected participation.

Tobie’s note

Make the next shared action clearer without turning a reminder into a public record of who failed.

02 · Reframing

Reduce the burden instead of building a bigger inventory.

A complete inventory depends on people continually entering and maintaining information. That can add work for the person already doing the organising. I shifted toward moments that need coordination: putting something in, checking or handling it, shopping and moving out.

Put in

Declare a plan

Capture the chosen plan rather than demand a complete inventory.

Check

See what needs attention

Group by area rather than attaching a problem label to a person.

Coordinate

Respect ownership

Seeing an item does not give someone permission to dispose of it.

03 · From findings to features

Every feature walks back to a behaviour someone described.

After coding the five interviews into behaviour cards, I identified nine ways a shared fridge fails (FP1–FP9). Each is a pattern seen across interviews rather than a single anecdote, and each names the interviews that produced it, so it can be checked.

Each feature in the build answers one of them. FP2 — identical packaging with no owner occupying space for months — became a found-something entry that locks ownership to unknown with a 48-hour hold. FP9 — a user withdrawing to avoid conflict — became a four-step move-out handover.

Tobie’s note

If a feature cannot be walked back, I mark it as a design judgement rather than a finding.

04 · Interaction rules

Location, ownership and permission are separate.

I separated where an item is, who claims it and what someone else may do with it. Unclaimed items retain unknown ownership. Neither a location nor a photograph automatically establishes an owner or permission to act.

Shelves belong to people, but the shelf an item sits on does not decide whose it is: my flatmate Xiaoman’s jam on my shelf is still Xiaoman’s, and I cannot dispose of it. The character describes situations without judging people. The interface does not determine food safety; judgement and action remain with the person.

05 · Physical & digital

Put the entry where the action happens.

Add and Manage are two clear entry points on the fridge door: record an intention when putting something away, or review what is already there. NFC links and a QR fallback connect the physical prompt to the detailed phone flow. The NFC entry was read-tested, and no read failed.

The penguin gives reminders a caring tone. I used AI-assisted visual iteration, then selected and refined a consistent character system.

The character was iterated with a generative image tool. The written specification came before the images, and each round rewrote the prompt rather than re-rolling the same one. The first two rounds were refused outright — one reason on record is that they read as generic AI mascot art — and the flat fourth round was carried into the expression system and the printed pieces. Because the specification came first, refusing a render was a documented decision rather than a matter of taste.

06 · Productising

One fridge, one tenant.

The web prototype from the exhibition (v1.8) has no server: every record lives on one phone, so what flatmate A logs, flatmate B cannot see. So I built v2.0: people who share a fridge see the same data, and people at any other fridge see none of it. This version is still in progress.

Joining goes through a sticker on the fridge. The QR code and the NFC tag carry the same link; if you can scan it, you are standing at the fridge. I considered requiring an admin’s approval and left it out for now: when someone moves out, the sticker is replaced and the old one stops working at once.

No record of who did it. Even with accounts, the subject of “leave it for now” and “dealt with” is still “someone”. An event records which fridge, which item, what happened and when. I considered logging the person to make reviews easier and decided against it: a permanent record of who handled what is a behaviour history. How many items were logged each week, how many were handled in time and how many people are still using it in week two can all still be counted.

Personal items show the owner’s name. “Ask me first” only works if you know whom to ask. Only the owner can switch “anyone can have this” on or off; when someone leaves, their items become “not sure whose”. The last two rules only surfaced when two accounts were walked through together.

Location photos are not uploaded. A photo stays on the phone that took it.

The first invitation on the live version failed. Once a fridge was created the link could not be retrieved again, and the people invited saw only “Create a fridge” after logging in, so each created their own. I changed it so that any member can get the current invite link at any time; someone who has not joined yet sees “Paste an invite link to join” first, and creating a fridge moved to a secondary entry.

In September 2026 v2.0 was tried in a five-person shared flat: I told my flatmates on the 15th, and people started using it on the 19th and 20th. They want it to keep developing, and they all like the penguin character.

Tobie’s note

Isolation lives in the database, not in the front end’s good behaviour. Not recording who did it is built into the tables, not left to a promise.

07 · 3D prototype

The fridge itself is the interface.

In November 2026 I turned the next version’s home screen into a fridge you handle directly: open the door, pick something up, drag it to another shelf, or feed it to the penguin. Every gesture maps to something the product already does.

Eat something and the penguin gets a fish. Go a week without anything spoiling and a new magnet appears on the door, free to move and turn.

Tobie’s note

Reminders come from the penguin and the magnets on the door, not from push notifications.

08 · Next iteration

Observe use before claiming effectiveness.

The next iteration would test whether first-time users understand the plan-based framing, then compare character directions and NFC entry points. The comparison materials are printed and ready.

I would also seek a household that successfully maintains a shared inventory. The existing sample describes failure more fully; a counterexample could clarify which complexity is useful and which can be removed.
